items.title: Computational and experimental strategies for functional validation of non-coding variants in pancreatic cancer.
items.summary: Journal: Functional & integrative genomics. Abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a highly aggressive malignancy characterised by extensive genomic heterogeneity and limited therapeutic options. Although recurrent coding mutations in key driver genes have been well researched, large-scale sequencing studies have identified a broad array of non-coding variants which may contribute to tumorigenesis by interfering with gene regulatory mechanisms. However, understanding the functional significance of these variants remains a major challenge due to their abundance and the complexity of non-coding regulatory structures. This review outlines current computational and experimental techniques to identify, prioritise, and functionally validate non-coding variants in PDAC. We discuss in silico methods including genome-wide association study (GWAS) fine-mapping, colocalisation, machine learning-driven functional annotation, and the use of established computational tools, in addition to epigenomic profiling technologies including, ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq, and CUT&RUN which define regulatory landscapes. We also emphasise new AI-based methods involving radiogenomics, AI imaging analysis and data integration, which provides novel potential to link genomic variation with phenotypic and imaging characteristics. Additionally, we highlight experimental validation techniques including reporter assays, electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSA), chromatin conformation capture methods, and CRISPR-based perturbation systems used to study variant functionality. Together, these complementary approaches establish a framework for correlating non-coding variation to regulatory mechanisms in PDAC.
items.headline: Computational and experimental strategies for functional validation of non-coding variants in pancreatic cancer
items.brief: This review discusses computational and experimental methods to identify and validate functional non-coding variants in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). It covers in silico techniques like GWAS fine-mapping, colocalization, machine learning-driven annotation, and epigenomic profiling methods such as ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq to define regulatory elements. The work addresses challenges in interpreting the vast non-coding variant landscape affecting gene regulation in PDAC.
items.why: It provides a comprehensive, rigorous overview of computational genomics and epigenomics methods tailored to non-coding variant functional analysis in a cancer context, directly relevant to computational genomics research.

items.title: Artificial intelligence aids multi-omics data integration in cancer drug discovery and development: from targets to drug synergy.
items.summary: Journal: Acta pharmacologica Sinica. Abstract: The emergence of multi-omics technologies has enabled the integration of genomic, transcriptomic, epigenomic, proteomic, and metabolomic data to characterize the molecular complexity of cancer. Single-cell and spatial profiling further resolve intratumoral heterogeneity, cell-cell interactions, and the microenvironmental determinants of therapeutic responses. In parallel, artificial intelligence (AI) provides computational approaches for integrating these heterogeneous data types across target identification, drug response prediction, toxicity assessment, and drug-combination modeling. Across these domains, the available evidence indicates that multi-omics integration is most beneficial when the included layers provide complementary biological information; that single-cell and spatial omics analyses reveal treatment-resistant populations and niches but remain largely research-grade and thus not ready for routine clinical deployment; and that although foundation models support some representation-learning tasks, their advantages in perturbation-response prediction require confirmation via stringent evaluation. By distinguishing externally validated advances from retrospective proof-of-concept studies, we provide a practical framework for evaluating the translational readiness of AI-driven multi-omics tools in precision oncology.
items.headline: Artificial intelligence aids multi-omics data integration in cancer drug discovery and development: from targets to drug synergy
items.brief: This article reviews AI methods for integrating multi-omics data—genomic, transcriptomic, epigenomic, proteomic, and metabolomic—to characterize cancer complexity. It highlights AI’s role in target identification, drug response prediction, toxicity assessment, and drug combination modeling. The review notes that foundation models support some representation learning tasks but their advantages in perturbation prediction remain limited, emphasizing the complementary value of diverse omics layers.
items.why: It rigorously surveys AI-driven multi-omics integration approaches in cancer, relevant for computational genomics and biological foundation models, emphasizing challenges and opportunities in drug discovery.

items.title: Explainable AI identifies recombination and chromatin environment as key predictors of subgenome evolution in maize and Brassica.
items.summary: Journal: Science advances. Abstract: Polyploidy, or whole genome duplication, reshapes genomes through biased gene loss and regulatory rewiring, yet the drivers of biased fractionation among subgenomes remain unclear. Using maize and Brassica rapa as model allopolyploids, we compiled 60 genomic and epigenomic features in maize and 45 in B. rapa and constructed supervised machine learning models to classify genes by subgenome identity. In both species, eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) approaches identified recombination rate as the most influential and highly interconnected feature despite nonsignificant mean differences between subgenome groups. Chromosome location, transposon density, and chromatin-associated features, including the proximity of accessible chromatin regions to genes and active histone marks such as H3K9ac and H3K27ac, consistently ranked among the top contributors to subgenome classification. XAI-derived covariation and interaction networks further revealed recombination rate as the central node connecting significant features. Together, these results highlight recombination and chromatin environment as major predictors of subgenome divergence in polyploid genomes.
items.headline: Explainable AI identifies recombination and chromatin environment as key predictors of subgenome evolution in maize and Brassica
items.brief: Using maize and Brassica rapa allopolyploids, this study compiles genomic and epigenomic features to classify genes by subgenome identity via supervised machine learning and explainable AI (XAI). It finds recombination rate as the most influential feature, interconnected with chromatin marks like H3K9ac and H3K27ac, transposon density, and accessible chromatin regions. The work links chromatin environment and recombination to biased gene loss and regulatory rewiring in subgenomes, providing mechanistic insights into 3D genome evolution.
items.why: It applies interpretable machine learning to integrate chromatin and genomic features, revealing key epigenomic determinants of subgenome evolution, directly relevant to computational epigenomics and regulatory element analysis.

items.title: Early self-regulation in context: Multidimensional organization of neonatal non-nutritive sucking and its association with subclinical maternal depressive traits.
items.summary: Journal: Journal of experimental child psychology. Abstract: From the very first days of life, infants' affective regulation unfolds within a dyadic co-regulatory system shaped by caregiver responsivity. In contexts of reduced maternal availability, such as maternal depressive states, infants may be required to compensate for diminished interpersonal regulation by increasingly relying on their internal resources. Neonatal non-nutritive sucking (NNS) represents one of the earliest spontaneously available regulatory behaviors, contributing to physiological and behavioral homeostasis from birth. However, it remains unclear whether its spontaneous organization is associated with early relational vulnerability indexed by maternal depressive symptoms. The present study aimed to characterize the spontaneous organization of NNS in a sample of newborns (N = 42) and to examine whether individual differences in NNS are associated with maternal postnatal depressive subclinical traits measured using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). Results from an exploratory principal component analysis indicated that neonatal sucking behavior was organized along two functional dimensions, reflecting overall sucking effort and behavioral activation, and the temporal organization of sucking bursts. Importantly, higher maternal depressive traits, though subclinical, were selectively associated with increased sucking effort, with infants of mothers reporting higher depressive traits showing more frequent and intense sucking, while no differences emerged for the organizational dimension. Overall, these findings suggest that individual differences in maternal depressive traits within the subclinical range may be associated with neonatal NNS effort, a precocious compensatory mobilization of regulatory resources, potentially serving both to support autonomous regulation and to elicit maternal engagement.
items.headline: Early self-regulation in context: Multidimensional organization of neonatal non-nutritive sucking and its association with subclinical maternal depressive traits
items.brief: This study examines neonatal non-nutritive sucking (NNS), an early regulatory behavior, and its association with maternal subclinical depressive symptoms. Using principal component analysis, the authors characterize the spontaneous organization of NNS in newborns and find that individual differences in NNS correlate with maternal postnatal depressive traits, suggesting early infant self-regulation is influenced by maternal affective context.
items.why: It offers an intriguing developmental neuroscience perspective linking early epigenetic-like regulation of infant behavior to maternal psychological states, relevant for evolutionary psychology and neurodevelopmental computational models.

items.title: Waist inequality and a Hurewicz-type theorem for mean dimension
items.summary: We establish a Hurewicz-type inequality relating mean dimension and conditional metric mean dimension. For every equivariant continuous map between dynamical systems, the mean dimension of the domain is bounded above by the sum of the mean dimension of the target and the conditional metric mean dimension of the map. In particular, any equivariant continuous map that decreases mean dimension must have infinite topological conditional entropy. The key ingredient is a new waist inequality, which we believe is of independent geometric interest beyond its application to dynamical systems. Compared with Gromov's original waist inequality, a distinctive feature of this inequality is that it applies to finite simplicial complexes of arbitrary topology, subject only to dimensional restrictions.
items.headline: Waist inequality and a Hurewicz-type theorem for mean dimension
items.brief: This paper proves a Hurewicz-type inequality relating mean dimension and conditional metric mean dimension in dynamical systems. It shows that for any equivariant continuous map, the mean dimension of the domain is bounded by the sum of the mean dimension of the target and the conditional metric mean dimension of the map. The authors also establish a new waist inequality applicable to finite simplicial complexes of arbitrary topology, which may have broader geometric implications beyond dynamical systems.
items.why: It advances rigorous mathematical foundations of mean dimension theory and provides a novel geometric inequality, valuable for researchers in computational topology and dynamical systems.

items.headline: This Is Your Brain on Art
items.brief: This New York Times article explores how engaging with art affects brain function, highlighting neuroscience research on aesthetic experience, emotional response, and cognitive processing during art perception. It discusses how art activates reward circuits and modulates attention and memory, providing insights into the biological basis of artistic appreciation.
items.why: It offers a rigorous synthesis of neuroscience findings on art perception, relevant for computational genomics researchers interested in neuroscience and evolutionary psychology of aesthetics.
